Blackstone stock draws EUR 13 billion for European credit fund
sum: Blackstone has raised around EUR 13 billion for its European direct-lending strategy, according to a report by Moneycontrol, which cited Bloomberg and published the report on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. Blackstone has closed its fourth European Senior Direct Lending Fund, targeting mid-market and upper-mid-market borrowers.

The fundraising gives Blackstone further scale in private credit, a business that provides fee income and expands the firm's lending capacity. The fund's focus covers companies in the middle and upper-middle segments of the European market, where borrowers typically seek financing outside traditional bank channels.

The fundraising comes as institutional investors continue to commit capital to large private-credit managers, even though the asset class has faced pressure in 2026. Moneycontrol reported concerns around redemption requests, software exposure, loan quality and private-asset valuations.

Brad Marshall, global head of private credit strategies at Blackstone Credit & Insurance, said the fundraising reflected investor confidence in private credit. He said investors were focusing on fundamentals rather than short-term market noise and viewed the lending backdrop as more attractive.

Blackstone's fund has already taken lead-lender roles in transactions involving Catalyst Pharmaceuticals, German regulatory-software company Regnology and residential-property manager Odevo, according to the report. Those examples show how the strategy is being deployed across healthcare, software and property-related lending.

For Blackstone, the fundraising supports the case for continued asset gathering and diversification beyond traditional buyout funds. It also keeps the company exposed to the central risks of private credit: borrower quality, valuation discipline and the ability of lenders to manage defaults or investor withdrawals.

Blackstone Mortgage Trust Q3 Earnings Call Highlights
sum: Blackstone Mortgage Trust BXMT reported a third-quarter GAAP net loss of $1.95 per share, while distributable earnings totaled $0.38 per share and distributable earnings before realized gains and losses were $0.42 per share. The company also reduced its quarterly dividend to $0.30 per share for the fourth quarter, from the $0.47 per share paid for the third quarter.

The fourth-quarter dividend will be payable Jan. 15, 2027, to stockholders of record as of Dec. 31, 2026. Chief Executive Officer Tim Johnson said the revised payout is intended to preserve capital, support long-term earnings power and provide flexibility for new investments, debt reduction or share repurchases.

“We set it to a level that we expect to cover in the fourth quarter of this year and in 2027,” Johnson said, adding that the company believes the dividend can be sustained across a range of interest-rate and credit environments.

Blackstone Mortgage Trust said it has accelerated portfolio turnover as higher interest rates have added pressure to certain investments originated before 2023. The company sold nearly $1 billion of loans since the prior quarter at a weighted-average price of $0.93 on the dollar relative to their carrying values at sale, according to management.

The sales included six legacy office loans totaling nearly $500 million and two legacy multifamily loans totaling approximately $200 million. Most of the sold loans had been on the company’s watchlist, contributing to a nearly 60% quarter-over-quarter reduction in watchlist loans, which management said reached their lowest level since 2019.

Including $250 million of loan sales completed during the quarter, the company collected $2.3 billion of repayments, its highest quarterly level since the fourth quarter of 2021. Nearly 90% of those repayments came from legacy loans. The company also received repayment of a $300 million legacy office loan in October that had been financed in the commercial mortgage-backed securities market.
Johnson said the company is on track to meet or potentially exceed its previously stated goal of reducing both office loans and legacy loans by 40% by year-end.

items.t: Blackstone’s Profits Fell, but Its Stock Rose 4%. Here’s What Dividend Investors See
sum: Blackstone just reported falling profits and its stock jumped 4%. That paradox reveals something about how asset managers pay dividends that most income investors never stop to examine.

Blackstone (NYSE:BX | BX Price Prediction) reported this morning that profit fell as rates, inflation, and a choppy market slowed dealmaking and investment exits (Bloomberg, Reuters). Investors still bought the stock, sending shares up 4.04% in early trading. That reaction explains why this group of stocks works for income investors. Asset managers collect fees on the money they manage, so rising markets lift assets, fees, and the cash that pays dividends. Blackstone, Franklin Templeton (NYSE:BEN) and Invesco (NYSE:IVZ) all pay their dividends from that fee engine, but each one sets its payout in a very different way.

An asset manager charges a small percentage fee on its assets under management (AUM). When stock and bond prices rise, AUM grows even if no new client money comes in, and fee revenue grows with it. At Invesco, the CFO said favorable markets alone added $257 billion to AUM last quarter. Alternative managers like Blackstone also earn performance fees and carried interest when they sell investments at a gain.

That income depends most on the market, because profitable exits need open IPO and M&A windows. It works in reverse too. Falling markets shrink AUM and fees, which is why all three stocks carry betas above 1.5: 1.587 for Blackstone, 1.576 for Franklin and 1.631 for Invesco.

Blackstone yields 4.88%, based on $5.23 per share paid over the past year, with shares at $114. The company has no fixed quarterly dividend. Blackstone pays out about 85% of its distributable earnings each quarter, so the check changes every time. The last three payments were $1.49, $1.16, and $1.29.

Dividend safety: The second-quarter dividend of $1.29 came from distributable earnings of $1.52 per share, a payout of about 84.9%. On GAAP earnings of $4.45 per share, the trailing payout comes to about 117.5%. The policy is based on distributable earnings, and management says it plans to return 100% of cash earnings over time through dividends. The balance sheet holds $7.5 billion of embedded realization potential, or $6 per share, the highest level in four years.

sum: At President Trump’s urging, the Florida legislature redrew the state’s electoral maps in an effort to increase the number of Republicans in Florida’s Congressional delegation. One of the members targeted by the changes is Congresswoman Kathy Castor (D-FL), who represents the state’s 14th Congressional District. Republicans changed the borders of Castor’s district in May 2026. The new 14th Congressional District supported Trump over Harris by more than 10 points.

In an election where Republicans are facing political headwinds, flipping Castor’s seat is a top priority. No Going Back PAC, an offshoot of Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC, has spent at least $6.4 million opposing Castor.

About $2.4 million of No Going Back PAC’s spending, according to AdImpact, has gone toward broadcasting an ad that attacks Castor for buying stock in a financial company that bought up property in Tampa. “In Congress, Kathy Castor traded stocks in a Wall Street firm that bought more than 1,600 Tampa Bay homes, raising rents and pricing people out,” the narrator says. “Kathy Castor profited.”

Although the ad does not name the “Wall Street firm,” it cites a June 22, 2013, article published in the Tampa Bay Times. According to that report, Blackstone, a New York private equity firm, through its subsidiary Invitation Homes “spent more than $250 million acquiring 1,650 homes in the Tampa Bay area.”

One of MAGA Inc.’s largest donors is Blackstone CEO and co-founder Stephen A. Schwarzman, who donated $5 million to MAGA Inc. in December 2025 and another $5 million in September 2026. MAGA Inc., which funds No Going Back PAC, is now spending millions to attack Castor for buying Blackstone stock.

Castor’s investment in Blackstone was tiny. According to reports filed by the House of Representatives, Castor purchased Blackstone stock worth between $1,000 and $15,000 in February 2015. She added to her position in January 2019, although the combined value was still $15,000 or less. When Castor sold her position in Blackstone in March 2020, the value was still somewhere between $1,000 and $15,000. sum: Shares of KKR, Ares, and Blackstone fell sharply in premarket trading Wednesday after Switzerland's Partners Group Holding AG moved to restrict investor withdrawals from one of its flagship private equity funds, deepening concerns about liquidity across the $1.8 trillion private markets industry.

Partners Group, which oversees approximately $185 billion in assets from its base in Zurich, Switzerland, said it was capping redemptions from its $8.6 billion Global Value SICAV fund – a so-called evergreen private equity vehicle that allows periodic investor withdrawals – at 5% of net asset value per quarter.

According to CNBC, the move came after withdrawal requests reached an estimated 9.8% in the second quarter, well above the fund's standard threshold, according to a letter to investors reported by Bloomberg News. Partners Group shares plunged 17.7% on the session, touching a 52-week low.

The announcement rippled quickly across U.S.-listed alternative asset managers. KKR shares moved 6.8% lower before the open, while Ares Management dropped nearly 6.7%, Blackstone fell 5.2%, and Blue Owl Capital Inc. slid 5.2%, according to CNBC. Carlyle Group Inc. edged down 2.9%.

For months, the liquidity squeeze had been largely contained to private credit – the broad category of non-bank lending that boomed over the past decade. But Partners Group Chief Executive David Layton sees wider contagion taking place, telling Bloomberg Television that the redemption pressure first seen in credit vehicles is spreading into other asset classes.

"There are some idiosyncratic factors for this fund in particular, but indeed you do see investors broadly, after having redemption pressure within private credit for a number of quarters, now starting to redeem other asset classes," Layton said.

The arc of the crisis has been steep. In the first quarter, redemption requests across U.S. non-traded private credit vehicles reached as high as 41% of some funds' net asset values, according to Reuters, prompting a majority of managers to draw a hard line around the standard 5% quarterly withdrawal cap.

sum: The statute governing utility acquisitions in New Mexico is unmistakably clear: stock of a utility or utility holding company may only be acquired “with the prior express authorization” of the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (PRC). Whether regulators overseeing Blackstone’s proposed acquisition of the Public Service Company of New Mexico (PNM) enforce this statute remains an open question, but the law itself dictates that they should.

TXNM Energy, the utility holding company that owns PNM, agreed to be acquired by private equity giant Blackstone in May 2025. In a filing that was released earlier this month, TXNM announced plans to issue $800 million in new equity prior to the closing of the acquisition, which must be approved by the PRC. Of that total planned equity issuance, $400 million in TXNM shares were purchased by Blackstone through a private placement. The transaction closed in June 2025, just a month after the acquisition was disclosed. The New Mexico PRC did not authorize this purchase.

“This was not a technical oversight,” Mariel Nanasi, senior attorney and executive director at New Energy Economy, told the Prospect. “It was reckless disregard for New Mexico law and for the commission’s exclusive jurisdiction and authority.”
A spokesperson for Blackstone told the Prospect: “We strongly disagree with the positions taken in the motion and will refute them in a formal response at the earliest opportunity.”

The revealed transaction is the latest twist in the saga of Blackstone’s attempted purchase of a utility that will serve 800,000 customers in New Mexico and Texas, and which has run into vociferous opposition from consumer groups, amid broader consternation about rising utility rates and private takeovers of power companies.

Both Nanasi and Prosperity Works, another intervenor in the case, have asserted that since the transaction was explicitly tied to and executed as part of the merger agreement itself, it rises to the level of an acquisition step rather than an incidental investment. In the utility M&A space, routine equity financing amounts to a contractual obligation. Funding doesn’t come until regulators offer their seal of approval.

Where Will Brookfield Asset Management Be in 5 Years?
sum: Brookfield Asset Management (BAM -1.27%) is a large Canadian asset manager. It has a history spanning more than 100 years of investing in infrastructure on a global scale. The stock's 3.3% yield is roughly in line with U.S. peers like Blackstone (BX -1.23%) and BlackRock (BLK +0.61%). Brookfield Asset Management's price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 34 is in a similar range.

That sets up a very compelling growth story for investors. Brookfield Asset Management is planning to double the size of its business by 2030. If that happens, earnings and dividends are likely to increase materially. Here's what you need to know.

Before looking to the future, it is important to look to the past. In 2020, Brookfield Asset Management set out an ambitious goal to double the size of its business by 2025. In 2020, the company's fee-bearing capital stood at $277 billion. By November 2025, that figure had grown to roughly $580 billion. To be fair, it's easier to double the size of a business when it's smaller compared to when it's larger, but management has clearly demonstrated that it can expand the business.

As an asset management company, Brookfield Asset Management earns fees for managing other people's money. As such, more assets mean more income. The company's fee-related earnings rose from $1.32 billion in 2020 to a projected $2.7 billion or so in 2025. Double the assets, and you roughly double the earnings.

This is where the next big goal comes in. By 2030, the company aims to increase its fee-bearing capital to $1.2 trillion. Fee-related earnings are projected to grow to $5.8 billion. That represents a 16% compound annual growth rate for fee-bearing capital and 17% annualized growth for fee-related earnings. Along with this, distributable earnings, which are what backs the company's dividend, are projected to rise 18% a year.
Given the proven ability to hit internal growth targets and the valuation and dividend yield of the stock today, what happens if Brookfield Asset Management hits its goal?
Assuming Wall Street places a similar valuation on Brookfield Asset Management as it has today, 16% annual growth in fee-related earnings will double the figure in 4.25 years.

items.t: The financial earthquake coming in 2026 to southern Gran Canaria due to the sale of Blackstone hotels
sum: The financial landscape of southern Gran Canaria is preparing for an unprecedented shake-up. Hotel Investment Partners (HIP), the hotel arm of the US giant Blackstone, which also owns Holiday World in Maspalomas, has activated the legal machinery for its imminent stock market debut. Under the watchful eye of international markets, the company has begun its transformation from a Limited Liability Company (SL) to a Public Limited Company (SA), a technical step that serves as the final countdown to its IPO in 2026.

For local savers in the south of the island, this operation is more than just an economic headline; it's a historic opportunity. For the first time, residents and small investors in San Bartolomé de Tirajana and Mogán could acquire shares in the very resorts that define their everyday landscape, such as the Barceló Margaritas or the former IFA chain properties now managed by Lopesan. The operation, coordinated by the giants Citi and Morgan Stanley, seeks to capitalize on the success of a model that has professionalized hotel management in the islands following an investment of over €600 million.

HIP's management, led by Alejandro Hernández-Puértolas, is maintaining its dual-track strategy. This means that, while the details of the Initial Public Offering (IPO) are being finalized, Blackstone is not ruling out a direct sale to the highest bidder if the offer is sufficiently attractive. In this scenario, Singapore's sovereign wealth fund (GIC), which already holds 35% of the capital, emerges as the natural candidate to take full control, thus consolidating Asian interest in the Canary Islands' economic engine.

The impact of this divestment will be profound. If the IPO goes ahead, HIP—valued at around €6.500 billion—would become one of the major players on the Spanish stock exchange, bringing the name of the Canary Islands' tourist destinations to Bloomberg terminals worldwide. Following the success of Cirsa (owner of Holiday World Maspalomas), Blackstone seeks to repeat the strategy, demonstrating that southern Gran Canaria remains the crown jewel of its European portfolio.
